name: The Yellow Christmas Tree of Stanyan Street

location.address: 1221 Stanyan Street, in front of the house

story:
New Zealand Christmas trees flower red. This one flowers yellow. The yellow form began as a natural mutation, found on Motiti Island in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty in 1940, in a species that otherwise blooms crimson.

Victor Reiter got hold of a cutting in the late 1950s and his family planted it in front of their home at 1221 Stanyan Street, on the edge of Cole Valley. The local tree writer Mike Sullivan, writing in 2016, called it his favourite tree in the city and found it thriving more than seventy years after that first yellow plant turned up. In 2019 the Urban Forestry Council voted unanimously to make it an official Landmark Tree.

Its moment comes around Memorial Day, at the end of May, when it blooms, and the flowers can still cover it in late June. Every other New Zealand Christmas tree you pass in the city flowers red.

This is a front garden, not a park, and the right way to see it is from the public pavement on Stanyan Street, without stepping off it. Our pin marks the address rather than the trunk.

The city still lists it among its landmark trees, but the newest dated photograph we have found is from June 2012, when it was in full yellow flower. Nobody has published its girth. If you photograph it from the pavement in flower, send it to us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in early summer by its yellow flowers, where the city's other New Zealand Christmas trees bloom red. It stands in front of the house at 1221 Stanyan Street; look from the pavement.

best_time.label: late May into June, when it blooms yellow instead of red

name: The Canary Palms of Quesada Avenue

location.address: Quesada Avenue median, just west of 3rd Street

verified_sources: https://sfpublicworks.org/services/significant-and-landmark-trees (SF Public Works official list: 'Quesada Street Median (West of 3rd Street to dead end): 13 Canary Island Date Palms')
https://www.sanfranciscostory.com/quesada-gardens/ (fetched directly: median planted around 1920 with Canary Island Date Palms, same as Dolores Street; palms survived the twentieth century)
access: Free, public street median in the Bayview; walk along the sidewalk.

Pin: Nominatim places Quesada Avenue between roughly 37.7299,-122.3854 and 37.7331,-122.3911; I set an approximate mid-block point, NOT checked on aerial imagery. lifecheck NONE at pin: alive evidence is only the official list and undated-recent articles; flag. story:
Thirteen Canary Island date palms line the median of Quesada Avenue in the Bayview, and San Francisco counts all thirteen as one Landmark Tree. Public Works lists them that way: the Quesada Street median, from just west of 3rd Street to the dead end, 13 palms.

They are the same species as the far better known palms down the middle of Dolores Street. Local history has the Quesada median planted with them around 1920. One account puts it closer to 1932, and we have not been able to settle which, so call them roughly a century old, give or take a decade.

What they have seen since is most of the Bayview's twentieth century, and they outlasted all of it; the city's current landmark list still carries all thirteen. A palm of this kind holds no rings to count, and nobody has published the height or the girth of any of the thirteen, so the age rests on the planting date alone.

This is a street, not a park, and that is the appeal: the whole landmark stands on one compact block, so there is one place to go and thirteen trees to count. Walk the sidewalk rather than the median itself.

Our pin is a mid-block point that has not been checked against aerial imagery, so treat it as the street rather than a spot. The 3rd Street end is the easy one to find. If you know when these palms were really planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the row of thirteen Canary Island date palms down the median of Quesada Avenue, running west from 3rd Street to the dead end.
